item.text: The notes raise several separate questions about the command, Moses’ fear, the return to a staff, and the grammar of *sīratahā*. I’ll keep the differing reports and parses distinct.

[BURHAN:v3p215/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | We will return it to its former course means to its former course, with ʿalā understood before sīrata.
[BIQAI-FULL:v5p16/r11] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Moses naturally feared the serpent, and God’s command to take it was training him for what he would face before Pharaoh.
[BIQAI-FULL:v5p16/r12] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Sīra means way or state; God promises to restore the serpent to its former state as a staff, a promise that cannot fail.

[DURR-FULL:v5p564/r10] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid glosses the phrase as its original appearance.

[DURR-FULL:v5p564/r9] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas glosses its former course as its former state.

[BURSEVI:v5p289#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Sīra is a pattern or kind of going, figuratively a way or form; the accusative follows removal of a preposition and denotes the staff’s original shape.
[BURSEVI:v5p289#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Moses put his hand in the serpent’s mouth; it returned to a staff, with his hand in the familiar place between its forks. The sign prepared him not to fear its transformation before Pharaoh.
[BURSEVI:v5p289#2/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النبي عليه السلام | reports | A hadith says that a person who failed to pay zakat will be brought with that wealth appearing as a serpent.
[BURSEVI:v5p289#2/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Every body, including a nonphysical one, has a spirit; each deed, trait, or attribute has a fitting form that becomes perceptible in the next life, as 6:108 says God will show people what they did. | mentions 6:108
[BURSEVI:v5p289#2/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Love of wealth is a powerful trait of the commanding soul, which resembles a harmful serpent and becomes an alarming form around its owner’s neck when inner realities are exposed.
[BURSEVI:v5p289#2/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | When the heart is purified from love of wealth and comes to love spending in God’s way, that disposition takes a beautiful form suited to its good deeds; the same analogy applies to other traits.
[BURSEVI:v5p289/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | An unattributed Persian couplet counsels abandoning base worldly existence to find love’s alchemy and become gold.
[BURSEVI:v5p289/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · المولى الجامي | reports | Jāmī says knowledge without action is poison and futile: one who knows alchemy has gained nothing unless he turns his own copper into gold.
[BURSEVI:v5p289/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Qāla is a resumption answering an implied question about what God did next.
[BURSEVI:v5p289/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The staff became a male serpent that swallowed rocks and stones in its path, had eyes blazing like fire and loudly grinding fangs, and stretched forty or eighty cubits between its jaws; Moses fled from the terrifying sight.
[BURSEVI:v5p289/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Moses feared because fear and flight from snakes and similar creatures belong to ordinary human nature.
[BURSEVI:v5p289/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Asked why Moses feared the staff while Abraham did not fear the fire, Bursevī says Abraham was more firmly established; God removed Moses’ initial fear, enabling him to take the staff and reach Abraham’s state of firmness.
[BURSEVI:v5p289/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The Prophet likewise first feared Gabriel, then became ready to see him in his true form on the Miʿrāj, as described in 53:13–14. | mentions 53:13, 53:14
[BURSEVI:v5p289/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · التأويلات النجمية | reports | The inward reading says Moses first believed the staff held benefits, then feared its harm; taking it without fear teaches that God alone brings harm and benefit, so fear and hope belong to Him alone.
[BURSEVI:v5p289/r9] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · المثنوي | reports | A Mathnawī couplet teaches that whoever fears God and adopts piety is feared by jinn and humans, while one who beholds God need fear no creature.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p177#4/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | After stopping in reverence and returning in great fear, Moses is told to take the serpent; fear is a natural human response to such a sight and does not diminish prophetic rank.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p177#4/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās reports that Moses was called to take it three times and only took it after the third call; Makkī says the third call included the promise to restore it. [ALUSI-FULL:v16p177#4/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās reports that the serpent was male.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p177#4/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · وهب | reports | Wahb reports that God specified that Moses take the serpent with his right hand.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p177#4/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | One view explains Moses’ fear as a response to a terrifying event directly from God whose nature he had not yet understood; Abraham did not fear the fire because it came through God’s enemy and its nature was clear.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p177#4/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Another view says Moses feared because he knew that a member of this species had played a part in Adam’s expulsion from Paradise.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p177#4/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Coordinating the prohibition with the command signals that not fearing is independently intended, rather than merely instrumental to taking the serpent.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p177#4/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | After Moses takes it, God will restore the serpent to its former staff-state; that promise explains why Moses should obey and not fear.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p177#4/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | A proposed wisdom is that the transformation, command to take it, and prohibition of fear prepare Moses for what will happen with Pharaoh; al-Ālūsī says this may underlie the claim that the promise is a further reassurance and sign, though that reading is not clear.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p177#4/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · وهب | reports | Aḥmad and others transmit from Wahb that Moses first covered his hand with his wool garment; an angel asked whether it would protect him if God allowed harm, Moses admitted his weakness, then put his hand in the serpent’s mouth and grasped its jaws; it became his familiar staff again. 70 · author | holds | Sīra derives from travel and first meant the form or state of a journey, then broadened to a general manner or state; it can mean a way or school, as in the cited line about a manner one has followed.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p178/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الحوفى | reports | Al-Ḥawfī’s analysis treats سِيرَتَهَا as a second object with a preposition omitted, originally إلى سيرتها or لسيرتها; Ibn Mālik adopts this analysis and Ibn Hishām approves it.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p178/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الزمخشرى | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī allows اعاد from عاده, meaning “return to it,” to govern two objects directly; the cited line by Zuhayr uses عادك to mean “turned you away.”
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p178/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الأصمعى | reports | Al-Aṣmaʿī and other lexicographers attest that عاد can take a direct object with the sense of turning or returning, supporting the transitive analysis.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p178/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو البقاء | reports | Abū al-Baqāʾ analyzes سِيرَتَهَا as an appositive of inclusion replacing the object pronoun in سنعيدها.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p178/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو حيان | rejects | Abū Ḥayyān rejects treating سِيرَتَهَا as an adverbial accusative because a specific manner is not an indefinite adverbial; a preposition في is needed, and omission is only poetic or anomalous.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p178/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · نحاة المغرب | reports | Grammarians of the Maghrib classify derived nouns such as مذهب as an indefinite type of adverbial, without distinguishing those ending in tāʾ; on their analysis this accusative is neither anomalous nor forced.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p178/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الزمخشرى | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī prefers parsing سنعيدها as complete on its own and سِيرَتَهَا as an absolute object of an understood verb: “we will restore it, moving in its former manner,” as when Moses leaned on it and used it for his flock.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p179/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | prefers | Al-Ālūsī says the Zamakhsharī parsing is good in meaning, with the implied participial clause either circumstantial or a new sentence, but it departs from the immediately apparent construction.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p179/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The verse indicates that a thing may change its reality, as when a staff becomes a serpent; divine creative command can bring this about.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p179/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعضهم | rejects | Some deny that a reality can turn into another, calling alteration of essences impossible and therefore outside the scope of divine power; al-Ālūsī rejects this denial.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p179/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعض المحققين | reports | One account of transformation is that God creates gold in place of the copper; another, held by some theologians who regard atoms as alike in accepting attributes, removes copper’s property and creates gold’s property. [TABATABAI:20:21-22/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Khawf is taking precautions against harm; khashya is inner agitation and disturbance of the heart.
[TABATABAI:20:21-22/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Prophets may experience ordinary fear but not khashya understood as a blameworthy weakness incompatible with courage; 33:39 says messengers fear none but God. | mentions 33:39

[ASAD-NOTES:20:21/r1] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | God tells Moses to take the snake without fear and promises to restore the staff to its original state.
